edition.locus: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia (archive bub_gb_DY2xvRwPetMC), Latin column, Duodecim Capita de Fide, Cap. X, printed p. 5 (PDF p. 29)

source_text: Si quis dicat, partem duntaxat hominis assumpsisse Christum, et non confitetur ipsum per omnia similem nobis, excepto peccato; anathema esto. Quomodo potest quisquam dicere, partem tantummodo hominis assumpsisse Christum? cum ipse Dominus dicat: Animam meam pono, ut iterum eam accipiam, pro ovibus meis. Et caro mea vere est cibus, et sanguis meus vere est potus: et, qui manducat meam carnem, et bibit meum sanguinem habet vitam aeternam.
thought_title: Christ took the whole of our humanity, not a part
orientation: Gregory condemns the view that Christ took only part of a man, since he lays down his soul and gives his flesh and blood.
pass_a_gloss: If anyone says Christ [to have] assumed (assumpsisse) only (duntaxat) a part (partem) of man, and does not confess him in all things (per omnia) like (similem) us, sin excepted (excepto peccato); let him be anathema. How can anyone say Christ assumed only (tantummodo) a part of man? when the Lord himself says: My soul (animam) I lay down (pono), that I may receive (accipiam) it again, for my sheep. And my flesh (caro) truly is food (cibus), and my blood (sanguis) truly is drink (potus): and, who eats (manducat) my flesh, and drinks my blood has eternal life.

choices.why: The argument is that Christ took a human soul as well as flesh and blood.
Same verb as assumptum in section 3.

pass_b_english: If anyone says that Christ took up only a part of man, and does not confess that he was like us in all things, except for sin (Hebrews 4:15), let him be anathema.

How can anyone say that Christ took up only a part of man, when the Lord himself says, “I lay down my soul for my sheep, so that I may take it again” (John 10:15; John 10:17)? And, “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John 6:55); and, “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” (John 6:54).
notes: Anima rendered “soul”, not “life”, because the argument is that Christ took a human soul as well as flesh and blood; the Gospel's sense “life” stands behind it.
The first saying joins John 10:15 (animam meam pono pro ovibus) and John 10:17 (ut iterum sumam eam); English order of the clauses adjusted.
Assumpsisse rendered “took up”, the same verb used for assumptum in section 3.
Hebrews 2:17 (“made like his brothers in all things”) is a parallel to the anathema.
